title: America Just Decided Who Gets to Use the World's Most Powerful AI. India Had to Ask Not to Be Left Out.
excerpt: Washington restricted Anthropic's Fable 5 and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 over security fears. India's top tech official flew to the Pax Silica Summit to secure a promise: trusted partners won't face 'abrupt cutoffs.'
body:
Washington has started picking who gets to use the world's most powerful AI. India just asked to be on the list — and got a qualified yes.

In a week that saw America's two leading AI companies forced to restrict access to their latest models over national security concerns, India quietly secured assurances from Washington that it will not be locked out of frontier artificial intelligence. The negotiations, described by a senior U.S. official as involving "sensitive national security" discussions, mark a new chapter in the technology relationship between the world's two largest democracies — one that could shape who gets to build with the most advanced AI systems for years to come.

What Happened

Two things collided in Washington this week.

On Friday, Anthropic announced that the U.S. government had partially reversed a two-week-old order blocking all access to its most powerful AI models — Claude Mythos 5 and Fable 5. More than 100 "trusted" U.S. organizations, including Fortune 500 companies, can now use Mythos 5 again. Fable 5 remains restricted. The original June 12 export control directive had barred all foreign nationals from using either model, an unprecedented intervention that forced Anthropic to shut down access entirely.

Hours earlier, OpenAI disclosed that it was delaying the public launch of GPT-5.6 at the U.S. government's request, limiting initial access to a small group of vetted partners. "We don't believe this kind of government access process should become the long-term default," OpenAI said in a blog post. "It keeps the best tools from users, developers, enterprises, cyber defenders and global partners who need them."

Together, the two moves signal that Washington is treating frontier AI models the way it has traditionally treated advanced weapons systems and nuclear technology: as strategic assets that require export controls and government approval before they leave the country.

India's Response: Don't Cut Us Off

At the second Pax Silica Summit in Washington on Thursday — a U.S.-led initiative to build trusted AI and semiconductor supply chains, now backed by 35 nations — India's top technology official made the country's position clear.

S. Krishnan, Secretary of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), told attendees that India had raised concerns directly with American officials about the reliability of access to advanced AI models such as Anthropic's Claude.

"We sought an understanding of how exactly the US is looking at this particular aspect and what their concerns are and how, in the future, this could be a reliable source of technology," Krishnan said. "If it is something which is to be used and made available, we can't have abrupt cutoffs."

Krishnan said the U.S. provided assurances that for "trusted partners, access will not be an issue" going forward.

Jacob Helberg, U.S. Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs and the architect of the Pax Silica initiative, confirmed the ongoing dialogue. "These are very sensitive national security discussions," Helberg said, adding that the U.S. intends to pursue a "gradual, measured approach" to releasing Anthropic's models "in a way that is safe, both for ourselves but also for our Indian counterparts."

Why This Matters for India's Tech Sector

India's concern is not abstract. The country is rapidly integrating AI across healthcare, financial services, education, manufacturing, and government services. Its $250-billion IT services industry — anchored by companies like Infosys, TCS, Wipro, and HCLTech — is betting its next growth cycle on AI-driven automation and enterprise transformation. Thousands of Indian startups are building products on top of frontier models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google.

An abrupt cutoff — whether driven by geopolitics, export controls, or a provider's commercial decisions — could cripple projects midstream, disrupt clients, and undermine India's positioning as a global AI services hub.

The fear is not hypothetical. When Anthropic shut down Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on June 12, it affected users worldwide, including Indian developers and companies building on the platform. No warning was given. The models simply went dark.

"Such interruptions in foundational AI technologies could arise due to geopolitical developments, export control regulations, or commercial decisions by providers, potentially affecting long-term AI-driven initiatives and digital infrastructure," Indian officials noted at the summit.

The Bigger Picture: AI as the New Arms Race

The restrictions on Anthropic and OpenAI reflect a deepening tension in Washington between promoting American AI dominance and controlling who gets to benefit from it.

Experts have warned that Mythos 5, in particular, could dramatically accelerate sophisticated cyberattacks by finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities faster than human security teams can patch them. The same capabilities that make frontier models valuable for cybersecurity defence make them dangerous in the wrong hands.

But critics argue that the government's approach — handpicking which companies and countries get access — creates more problems than it solves. "No one knows how these companies are picked and why everyone else is excluded," said John Coleman of the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman echoed the concern on X: "I just don't like the idea of the government picking the customers."

For India, the question is whether it can secure a seat at the table before the rules are set in stone. At the Pax Silica Summit, 35 nations signed the Joint Statement on AI Opportunity, committing to a "pro-growth, pro-innovation regulatory approach" and trusted supply chains for AI infrastructure.

India signed. But signing a statement and securing guaranteed access to the models that actually power AI are two different things — and New Delhi knows it.

What Comes Next

The immediate question is when Fable 5 — Anthropic's general-purpose model, designed for wide public use — will be restored. The government is "moving towards" allowing its release, according to a person familiar with the matter, though no timeline has been set.

For India, the longer play is about diversification. Officials have begun discussing how to build resilient AI supply chains that do not depend on a single provider or a single country's regulatory decisions. That means investing in domestic AI capabilities, exploring partnerships with multiple model providers, and pushing for multilateral frameworks that prevent any one government from unilaterally cutting off access to foundational technology.

The irony is not lost on anyone in New Delhi: India spent years building the world's largest IT outsourcing industry by becoming indispensable to American companies. Now, as AI rewrites the rules of that relationship, India finds itself on the other side of the dependency — asking Washington for assurances that the technology tap will not be turned off.
